why: Photoacoustic breast imaging is already an FDA-approved product, and a Caltech spin-out is commercialising whole-breast PACT, so this is an existing device pointed at screening.
found: Seno Medical's Imagio opto-acoustic/ultrasound breast system has FDA PMA approval (2021) for assessing breast masses; Lihong Wang founded a company to commercialise breast PACT.

why: A funded startup is already building organ-scale vitrification with uniform rewarming for transplant.
found: Until Labs raised a $58M Series A (Sept 2025, >$100M total) to vitrify donor organs and rewarm them uniformly, with large-animal organs and human trials in view.

why: Recovering organs an hour after circulation stops would widen the donor pool far beyond today's minutes-long window.
found: OrganEx (Yale, 2022) worked only in pigs; spin-out Bexorg perfuses brains for drug discovery, and no company is taking it to transplant.

why: LyGenesis is already running a Phase 2a trial that grows liver tissue in patients' lymph nodes.
found: LyGenesis Phase 2a (NCT04496479) dosed its first patient in March 2024 and is escalating doses through cohorts.

why: Editing a donor organ on the pump would let transplants go ahead without lifelong immunosuppression.
found: Only preclinical and feasibility work: AAV delivered to pig hearts during perfusion, and CRISPR feasibility in perfused human donor lungs; no company or human transplant.

why: Is a humanised kidney that has only reached day 28, with pig blood vessels, plausible enough for a card? My pick: keep.
found: Guangzhou group (Cell Stem Cell 2023) grew partly human mesonephros in pig embryos to day 28; no company or later-stage organ.

why: Amphix Bio is a funded startup taking this exact gel to spinal cord injury trials.
found: Amphix Bio's AMFX-200 got FDA orphan drug designation in July 2025, with first human trials targeted for late 2026.

why: Steering regrown fibres back to their old targets is what turned regrowth into walking after a complete cord injury.
found: EPFL/UCLA/Harvard Science 2023 work in mice, scaling to primates; no startup or trial for the gene therapy found.

why: Science Corp is a funded startup building a biohybrid implant whose grafted neurons grow into the brain.
found: Science Corp's biohybrid implant puts stem-cell-derived neurons on a chip; mouse prototypes grew into cortex, and its sensor is being prepared for first human use (2026).

why: Electronic bridges across a cut cord already exist; wireless grains are a better electrode for the same device.
found: ONWARD's brain-spine 'digital bridge' is in patients; Iota Biosciences (neural dust, Astellas), MintNeuro and Cahira are building wireless micro-implants.

why: The 2025 rat study it rests on gave modest functional gains and found no extra axon regrowth, so the steering mechanism is unsupported.
found: Chalmers/Auckland Nature Communications 2025: subdural field treatment improved rat function but did not change axon regeneration markers; nothing in humans.

why: Can a ground array of hundreds of megawatts of gyrotrons track a rocket and beat reusable chemical rockets enough to move toward $10/kg? My pick: keep.
found: Escape Dynamics folded in 2015 after thruster tests; only academic and JAXA work since, nothing being built.

why: HyperSciences (General Hypersonics) is building a reusable ram-accelerator tube aimed at launching payloads to space.
found: General Hypersonics flew two Mach 4+ ram-accelerator launches from one reusable tube in 2026 and plans payloads to the Karman line.

why: This is SABRE: Reaction Engines built and tested the precooler, and ESA's Invictus programme now carries the engine forward.
found: Reaction Engines tested SABRE precoolers before closing in 2024; ESA's Invictus (2025) is developing a precooled air-breathing hydrogen engine spaceplane.

why: Vaire Computing is a funded startup building resonator-driven reversible chips and has taped one out.
found: Vaire's Ice River test chip (22 nm, 2025) recovers energy through an LC resonator, about 30% less energy on one task; second tapeout under way.

why: Does the DARPA 3DSoC chip already fabricated at SkyWater count as this being built? My pick: drop.
found: SkyWater fabricates monolithic 3D chips stacking nanotube logic and RRAM in a commercial foundry under DARPA 3DSoC; CMU reported ~10x gains at IEDM 2025; no product.

why: Training by pulsing weights where they sit would cut the energy of AI training by orders of magnitude.
found: Only research arrays (MIT, IBM, Illinois); IEEE Spectrum says a commercial ECRAM training chip is still some way off; no startup found.

why: With no material yet switching at 100 mV and a read-out too weak to drive the next gate, is it plausible enough? My pick: keep.
found: Intel showed a single MESO device at IEDM 2021; no circuit or product since.

why: A plasma mass filter splits waste into heavy and light groups, not 60 pure elements, since neighbours like nickel, cobalt and copper differ by under 10%, and ionising everything costs megawatt-hours per tonne.
found: Only lab devices and proposals (PPPL, Gueroult/Fisch for NdFeB magnets); Archimedes never ran at scale; Radify uses plasma for reduction, not mass separation.

why: Pulling copper out of molten scrap would let old scrap make top-grade flat steel instead of rebar.
found: University of Toronto (Azimi) reported the first electrochemical removal of copper from molten steel below alloy level with an oxysulfide electrolyte; no startup or pilot.

why: Turning unsorted polyolefin waste into virgin-grade propylene would close the loop on most plastic.
found: Berkeley Science 2022 tandem isomerising ethenolysis gave >80% propylene; only academic follow-ups, no pilot plant or company.
